rounds.title: ROUND 1 · JUST BEND IT
rounds.subtitle: Dry spaghetti · both ends clamped
rounds.question: How many pieces?
fact: The first snap sends a wave

explain.title: WHY?
lines: The snap sends a bending wave

source: Simulated: break pattern from these studies
caption: Try it: you can't snap dry spaghetti in two. 🍝 Bend it and it breaks into 3 pieces or more. Twist it about 270° first and it breaks cleanly in two. What should we test next? 👇 #spaghetti #physics #science #mit #satisfying #mythbusting #3danimation
description: Can you break a dry spaghetti into exactly two pieces? We clamp both ends and bend it until it snaps. Then we do it again, but twist it first.

Bent on its own, the spaghetti almost never breaks in two: it breaks into three pieces or more. When the first crack opens, the two halves suddenly spring back, and that sends a bending wave along each half. The wave bends the stick even more for an instant and breaks it again. Basile Audoly and Sébastien Neukirch explained this in 2005; Richard Feynman had spent an evening breaking pasta without finding the answer.

In 2018 an MIT team built a machine that clamps a spaghetti at both ends, twists it, then bends it, filmed at up to a million frames per second. Twisted by about 270 degrees first, the spaghetti breaks cleanly into two pieces: part of the stored energy escapes as a twisting wave, which leaves too little for a second break.
The animation is a simulation. The number of pieces follows these studies; the motion is slowed down enormously so you can see it.
sources_detail: B. Audoly and S. Neukirch, 'Fragmentation of rods by cascading cracks: why spaghetti does not break in half', Physical Review Letters 95, 095505 (2005).

R. Heisser, V. Patil, N. Stoop, E. Villermaux, J. Dunkel, 'Controlling fracture cascades through twisting and quenching', PNAS 115 (2018). MIT News (13 Aug 2018): bending alone usually gives three or more fragments; model predicts about 270 degrees of twist to break a stick in two (experiments used almost 360 degrees); clamps at both ends, one rotates, one slides to bend; cameras up to a million frames per second.
Simulated: 3 pieces when bent alone, 2 pieces when twisted 270 degrees first; motion illustrative and slowed down.
